this is part 1 of a list I'll compile for this sub. I like YouTube really well for DIY stuff, and this particular YouTuber has a large number of "how-to" videos as well as product review and "How I did it" videos. One of the nicest things about YouTube is that you can find reviews of almost any piece of equipment on YouTube, and watch them multiple times before deciding to buy.

One of the things I like about this particular poster is that (I've no doubt he's getting paid) he reviews Chinese machines, which have taken the market by storm. I know people don't like them (I don't have any), but the reviews are good enough to make me realize that these machines may be worth buying. Besides. ESAB sources quite a few products from China, so if you're going to "buy American," or "Buy European," you and I both know that we have to look at production location and parts sourcing--what with Milwaukee and Porter Cable now sourcing much of their tools from China.

ESABs build quality is actually quite impressive, they use higher end plants in China instead of cheap slave labor camps.

I've always been sold to Miller since I started 15 years ago, used to be only Lincoln & Miller had good after sales service in North America but that's changed now... actually starting to think Miller is riding on its reputation for high machine prices.

I bought a Tweco Fabricator 211i about 2 years ago, which is ESAB, and I think it's a wonderful machine. I got it as a garage welder and it runs amazingly, very stable whether doing short circuit or spray transfer. The torch feels sturdy for a smaller model, no big overheating issues. It runs stick fine & DC tig is decent enough... although nothing beats a Miller Dynasty for tig welding, I love my 200.

Thx for sharing the link, I always enjoy watching other welders techniques.

Glad to hear the kudos for ESAB. When I bought my Miller (2015), I was afraid of them because of their Chinese manufacture; turns out I probably should have bought the ESAB because it will do more. I have to work outside, so for me it's stick (Miller), fluxcore (Forney) and carbon arc torch (brazing only). At the present moment, I sorta wish I had bought the Lincoln 210MP, but it wasn't out yet, and selling my other stuff to buy that just doesn't make sense. I am also restricted to 110V until I can start using the garage, which will only happen when the dogs die. They are old, so maybe MIG and TIG are in my future after all...

That 210mp looks like a nice machine, small multi process is the fad right now for contractors, a lot more fun than running hundreds of feet of cable all the time. The only big downside I can see is the lack of high frequency for aluminum tig, a spool gun can only do so much in the field & forget fixing old oily cast parts.

As for being stuck with 110v, I got myself a 7500w gas & lp genset for 700$. Build a shed for it & cut the noise, no big wiring issues either. Both my machines run fine on it, I can even do side-jobs with it.

Union Army Lance Sergeant John Clem, age 12; the youngest non commissioned officer in American Army history and, as a Brigadier General, the last Civil War vet to retire. 1863

John Clem (1851 – 1937) was a United States Army general who served as a drummer boy in the Union Army in the American Civil War. He gained fame for his bravery on the battlefield, becoming the youngest non-commissioned officer in Army history.

At age 10 Clem tried to join the 22nd Michigan, which refused him due to his age and size. He tagged along anyway and the 22nd eventually adopted him as mascot and drummer boy. Officers chipped in to pay him the regular soldier's wage of $13 a month and allowed him to officially enlist two years later.

Clem served as a drummer boy for the 22nd Michigan at the Battle of Chickamauga. He is said to have ridden an artillery caisson to the front and wielded a musket trimmed to his size. In the course of a Union retreat, he shot a Confederate colonel who had demanded his surrender. After the battle, the "Drummer Boy of Chickamauga" was promoted to sergeant, the youngest soldier ever to be a non-commissioned officer in the United States Army.

In October 1863, Clem was captured in Georgia by Confederate cavalrymen while detailed as a train guard. The Confederates confiscated his U.S. uniform which reportedly upset him terribly—including his cap which had three bullet holes in it. He was included in a prisoner exchange a short time later, but the Confederate newspapers used his age and celebrity status for propaganda purposes, to show "what sore straits the Yankees are driven, when they have to send their babies out to fight us."

He retired from the U.S. Army in 1915, having attained the rank of brigadier general in the Quartermaster Corps. He was the last veteran of the American Civil War still on duty in the U.S. Armed Forces. By special act of Congress on August 29, 1916, he was promoted to major general one year after his retirement.
